title: The four groups of presidential appointees (Sec. 16; Mison)
ask: Name the four groups of presidential appointees and say which needs the Commission on Appointments.
items: Group 1 (CA consent): heads of executive departments; ambassadors, other public ministers and consuls; AFP officers from colonel or naval captain; officers whose appointments the Constitution vests in the President
Group 2: all other officers whose appointments are not otherwise provided for by law
Group 3: those the President may be authorized by law to appoint
Group 4: officers lower in rank whose appointment Congress vests in the President alone
Only group 1 needs CA consent; Congress cannot add to it (Calderon; Manalo)
src: Art. VII, Sec. 16; Sarmiento III v. Mison (1987)
hook: Four groups, one door to the CA.

title: Appointments that need no CA confirmation
ask: Give examples of presidential appointments that need no CA confirmation, with the authority.
items: Bureau heads, such as the Commissioner of Customs (Mison)
NLRC Chairman and Commissioners (Calderon)
Senior PNP officers (Manalo)
Coast Guard officers from captain up, after the transfer to the DOTC (Soriano)
Justices and judges from a JBC list (Art. VIII, Sec. 9)
The Ombudsman and Deputies from a JBC list (Art. XI, Sec. 9)
The VP as a Cabinet member (Art. VII, Sec. 3)
Acting secretaries, for up to a year (Pimentel v. Ermita)
src: Mison; Calderon; Manalo; Soriano; Pimentel v. Ermita

title: Regular, ad interim and acting appointments
ask: Distinguish regular, ad interim and acting appointments.
items: Regular: made while Congress is in session; effective after CA consent
Ad interim: made during a recess; effective at once; permanent (Matibag)
Ad interim ends only on CA disapproval or the next adjournment; a by-passed one may be renewed, a disapproved one may not
Acting: temporary, at pleasure; may be made even while Congress is in session; at most one year (Pimentel v. Ermita; Administrative Code, Book III, Sec. 17)
Acting appointments are barred for constitutional commissioners and for offices repugnant to them (Urro; Brillantes v. Yorac)
A by-passed ad interim appointment is not a prior term, so renewal is not reappointment (Matibag)
src: Matibag (2002); Pimentel v. Ermita (2005); General v. Urro (2011)
hook: Ad interim is permanent; acting is temporary.

title: The four elements of a valid appointment (Velicaria-Garafil)
ask: State the elements that must concur for a valid appointment.
items: Authority to appoint and evidence of its exercise
Transmittal of the appointment paper and evidence of the transmittal (release through the Malacañang Records Office)
A vacant position at the time of appointment
Receipt of the appointment paper and acceptance (oath or assumption) by an appointee with all the qualifications and none of the disqualifications
src: Velicaria-Garafil v. Office of the President (2015)

title: The election ban on appointments (Sec. 15)
ask: State the rules on the ban on midnight appointments.
items: From two months before the next presidential election to the end of the term
Binds only the President or Acting President (De Rama)
Exception: temporary appointments to executive positions when continued vacancies would prejudice public service or endanger public safety
Does not apply to the Judiciary; Valenzuela reversed (De Castro)
The whole process, including acceptance, must be complete before the ban (Velicaria-Garafil)
Inside the period, the appointment is void whatever the merit or motive
An Acting President’s appointments may be revoked by the elected President within 90 days (Sec. 14)
src: Art. VII, Secs. 14–15; De Castro; De Rama; Velicaria-Garafil
hook: President only, judges excepted, all four steps before the cut-off.

title: Terms in the constitutional commissions (Funa v. Villar; Gaminde)
ask: State the rules on the terms of members of the constitutional commissions.
items: Seven-year terms without reappointment; first appointees 7, 5 and 3 years
Terms run in a cycle from February 2, 1987; a late appointment loses the gap (Gaminde)
A vacancy from expiration of a term: a full seven years, never shorter (no split terms)
A vacancy from death, resignation, disability or impeachment: only the unexpired portion
No one may serve more than seven years in all
A Commissioner who resigns may be promoted to Chairman only into a seat vacated by death, resignation, disability or impeachment, within the seven-year total
No temporary or acting appointment or designation
src: Art. IX-B to D, Sec. 1(2); Gaminde (2000); Funa v. Villar (2012)
hook: February 2 clock; seven in all; no split terms.

title: Limits on the power to remove
ask: When can the President not remove a presidential appointee at will?
items: Impeachable officers: only by impeachment (Art. XI, Sec. 2)
Officers of an independent constitutional office: a Deputy Ombudsman (Gonzales III, 2014)
Officers with security of tenure: only for cause provided by law, with due process (Larin; Art. IX-B, Sec. 2(3))
Betrayal of public trust needs bad faith and gravity comparable to the impeachment grounds (Gonzales III, 2012)
A reorganization that abolishes posts must be in good faith; badges of bad faith void it (Larin; RA 6656, Sec. 2)
Acting appointees serve at pleasure: their separation is expiration, not removal (Urro)
src: Larin (1997); Gonzales III (2012, 2014); General v. Urro (2011)
hook: Appoint, then remove, unless impeachable, independent, or tenured.

title: The limits on the pardoning power
ask: When may the President not grant a pardon?
items: In cases of impeachment (Art. VII, Sec. 19)
Before conviction by final judgment: a pardon during appeal is void
For violations of election laws, rules and regulations without the COMELEC’s favorable recommendation (Art. IX-C, Sec. 5)
Congress cannot add limits by statute (Cristobal; Risos-Vidal)
The ConCom rejected, 34–4, a clause letting Congress limit clemency for corrupt-practices offenses
src: Art. VII, Sec. 19; Art. IX-C, Sec. 5; Risos-Vidal (2015)
hook: No impeachment, no appeal pending, no election offense without COMELEC; Congress adds nothing.

title: The forms of executive clemency
ask: Name the forms of clemency in Art. VII, Sec. 19, and say which needs Congress.
items: Reprieve: postpones the execution of a sentence
Commutation: reduces the sentence to a lighter one
Pardon: forgives the punishment, absolutely or on conditions
Remission of fines and forfeitures
Amnesty: erases the offense for a class of political offenders
Only amnesty needs the concurrence of a majority of all the Members of Congress

title: Pardon versus amnesty (Barrioquinto)
items: Pardon: by the President alone; amnesty: with the concurrence of Congress
Pardon: a private act that must be pleaded and proved; amnesty: a public act of which courts take judicial notice
Pardon: after conviction; amnesty: before or after prosecution, sometimes after conviction
Pardon: to an individual; amnesty: to classes of persons, usually for political offenses
Pardon looks forward and forgives the punishment; amnesty looks backward and erases the offense
Pardon restores office and suffrage only if it says so and never remits civil indemnity (RPC Art. 36)

title: What an absolute pardon does and does not do
ask: What does an absolute pardon do, and what does it not do?
items: Removes the penalty and the disqualifications based on the conviction (Cristobal)
Restores the right to vote and run if it restores “civil and political rights” (Risos-Vidal)
Restores eligibility for appointment to the forfeited office (Monsanto)
Does not restore the forfeited office itself: reappointment needed (Monsanto)
Gives no backpay: a pardon looks forward (Monsanto)
Does not remit civil indemnity (RPC Art. 36)
Does not erase guilt or restore reputation unless grounded on innocence (Monsanto)
hook: Forgiveness, not forgetfulness: rights yes; office, pay and reputation no.

title: Why Estrada could run after his pardon (Risos-Vidal)
ask: Why did the Court hold that Estrada’s pardon let him run for Mayor of Manila?
items: Only the Constitution limits the pardoning power; Congress cannot
RPC Arts. 36 and 41 only clarify that accessory penalties stay unless the President remits them
“Restored to his civil and political rights” expressly remitted them
The right to seek elective office is a political right
The Monsanto concurrences requiring specific words are not controlling
The whereas clause on his promise not to run is not a condition: a preamble is not operative
The plenary-pardon exception in OEC Sec. 12 lifts the LGC Sec. 40 disqualification
hook: Political rights include running; whereas is not a condition.

title: Breach of a conditional pardon (Torres v. Gonzales)
ask: State the three propositions on conditional pardons and their breach.
items: Granting a pardon and fixing its conditions are purely executive acts, not subject to judicial scrutiny
Breach may be determined by the President under RAC Sec. 64(i), with no conviction needed, or by a court under RPC Art. 159, which needs conviction by final judgment
The choice between the two is the President’s
Due process is not always judicial process: the convict had his day in court on the original crime
Recommitment only revives the remitted part of the old sentence; new crimes still need final convictions
hook: Two roads back: the President’s word or the court’s judgment.

title: Claiming an amnesty
ask: What must a person show to claim an amnesty?
items: The amnesty was granted with Congress’s concurrence (majority of all the Members)
He belongs to the class and the acts fall within its period and crimes
The acts were not excluded (e.g., crimes for personal ends)
He admits committing the covered acts (Vera: amnesty presupposes a crime)
He admits that the acts were criminal; he need not admit the specific crime charged (Trillanes)
src: Vera v. People (1963); Trillanes v. Medialdea (2024)
hook: Covered, then confess: no admission, no amnesty.

title: Why Proclamation No. 572 was void (Trillanes v. Medialdea)
ask: Give the grounds on which the Court voided the revocation of Trillanes’s amnesty.
items: Revocation of an amnesty needs the concurrence of Congress, as the grant does
Due process: the DND grant had become final and immutable, and he was not heard
Equal protection: all 277 grantees’ forms were missing, but only his amnesty was voided
Ex post facto: it stripped a vested protection against prosecution; the clause binds the Executive too
Double jeopardy: a dismissal on the ground of amnesty bars a new prosecution even on the accused’s motion
Not a bill of attainder, and no warrantless arrest was ordered
He did apply and did admit guilt, as the courts below found
hook: Congress again; then due process, equal protection, ex post facto, double jeopardy.
